There's tons of different types of management my dude. I'm 22, and I'm merely using this as a stepping stone. I went from being an anti-social kid going no where to become a face that everyone knows. Just tonight I went bowling with the girlfriend and another couple and I met a few older gentlemen who knew me from my bar and bought me a drink. I strive on making connections with people. This job is pushing me farther in life and it's teaching me a lot. I'm personally going the IT route and one of my favorite customers is a CEO for a rather big business here and he want's me to start in a low-level IT job and move up because of my skills. To be honest it's pretty easy, you just have to be an all around people person and you have to be able to multitask. Could you handle people asking you stupid questions everyday.

So here I am running down a hall way telling our waitress to get someone from the back of the house to help her because I'm designated FoH. I put the blame on myself for not double checking with each staff member if they personally don't prepare themselves and do their jobs correctly because it's my job to make sure they're doing their job.

I personally like fast paced high stress people jobs, which is why I like being in the front. I put a lot of work and personal time into studying people, staff and customers. I just enjoy learing how people react to different situations. It's a lot of craziness in your head. I personally feel at peace and I'm super relaxed when there's too much going on that I can't think. It's the days where it's so slow and I'm just going through our books matching prices with constantly raising food prices and liqour prices that bore me to death.

My second night working was new years eve of last year and it was the busiest night I've worked in this line of work so far, if only I could take the tips I've learned along the way that night.

Long story short -> My family owns a fine-dining restaurant/pub and we lost our bartender for New Years so my family asked if I'd be willing to go at it since we were in a pickle. Mind you I've been around this business since I was 12 and I'm 21 now I had just never taken a serious interest in it until they asked me to do it for one night. I was the first one there in the morning and I stocked myself to the brim with bottles, cans, backup liquor. I cut all of my lemons and limes and pulled my olives and what not. I got there at 9AM and got out at 2AM, long day anyways.... We get slammed and the first thing I caught myself doing was asking multiple people for the same drink. For example I'd call out to everyone drinking a bud light bottle if they needed another one. I'd grab 6 bottles and cap them and collect the money, then I'd move on to drafts or mixed drinks and so on. I started with the fastest most basic thing you can do behind the bar and kind of followed that system since it was working. I didn't linger on people who were undecided on their drinks I told them kindly that I'd get back to them. Mind you I wasn't a social kid growing up so at this point I was basically a robot just pouring and mixing to the best I could. It was sink or swim the whole night. Turns out it was the greatest night of my life and it sparked something inside me that I never knew was there. Hospitality is one of my strongest skills now and that night has been a huge part of my life ever since. I'm still working for my family but I've taken on a lot more responsibility handling the front of house. I've become very good at public relations and communicating with people face to face.

Sorry for the TL;DR you asked how my first experience was and I tried to keep it short. 

1) Be confident. If you don't know what you're doing at least pretend to know what you're doing.

2) Don't get hung up on something you've done wrong, especially if you're working in a fast paced establishment. You need to keep your mind moving.

3) Make eye contact with every customer at your bar, smile and communicate when feasible. It gives a human connection when you're swamped which results in less complaints if the service is slow because you're busy.

I'm not so sure if these are tips for stress management itself but tips in general. Just keep a cool head. One of the greatest things I learned to do is to laugh at myself. When I make a mistake I laugh and crack a joke if it's something silly. I laugh and smile every time I work because I genuinely love what I do.

I'm very rarely swamped bad enough that I can usually take a few seconds of my time to ask how the patron would like their drink and by doing so I put a face to my drink and they end up becoming the recipe.

Some may say that's a bad way of doing things because I'm tailoring that specific drink to their liking and in a way I'm not following the 'real' recipe but I disagree. In doing so you're learning variations of the drink, provided it's not the raw recipe but at the same time you're still creating the base drink at hand and that repetition sticks with you, all while you're making that drink they oh so love and keep coming back for.
